planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring into well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; 'Tuttlei' is a dense, low, nearly thornless selection commonly used for foundation plantings and low hedges along the Gulf Coast.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery containers in spring in sandy, well-drained soil, spacing plants to form a continuous low hedge or mass planting. This dwarf, mounding selection of Natal plum stays under two feet tall with few or no spines, producing smaller flushes of the same fragrant white, jasmine-like flowers and edible crimson fruit as the standard species, though fruiting is lighter than taller forms. It tolerates salt spray and reflected heat well, making it a durable choice for coastal foundation beds. Only fully ripe, deep-red fruit should be eaten; green fruit and foliage are not edible.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; 'Fancy' is an upright, heavier-fruiting selection grown specifically for its larger, better-flavored berries rather than hedge form.

directions: Plant in full sun on well-drained, sandy to loamy soil, allowing room for an upright, arching habit taller than typical landscape Natal plum selections. 'Fancy' is grown primarily as a fruiting cultivar, selected for larger, sweeter crimson berries that are well suited to fresh eating, jelly, and juice, and it tends to bear more consistently than seedling-grown plants. The spiny branching and fragrant white flowers are typical of the species, so site it away from foot traffic. Harvest fruit only when fully deep red and slightly soft, as unripe fruit and all other plant parts are toxic.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained sandy soil in full sun to light shade; 'Boxwood Beauty' is an extremely low, dense, nearly spineless form grown mainly as a formal edging or low border plant.

directions: Install rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, sandy soil, spacing closely for a tight, clipped-looking low border; this cultivar tolerates both full sun and several hours of afternoon shade without losing density. Its tiny, glossy leaves and compact, spineless mounding habit make it a popular boxwood substitute in frost-free coastal gardens, though flowering and fruit set are sparse compared with taller Natal plum forms. When fruit does form, the small red berries are edible once fully ripe, with the same tart-sweet flavor as the species. Prune lightly after flushes of growth to maintain its dense, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in sharply drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Vancouver Jade' spreads faster and tolerates garden conditions better than wild-collected bearberry.

directions: Set out container plants in spring on sharply drained, acidic, sandy soil, giving each plant room to spread into a dense, glossy mat. 'Vancouver Jade' was selected for faster establishment, denser bright-green foliage, and better tolerance of typical garden soils than the species as collected from the wild, while keeping its disease resistance and vigor. Small pink urn-shaped flowers appear in spring, followed by dull red berries that persist into winter as wildlife food and are edible but mealy and astringent for people. It performs well as a bank or slope cover under open conifers where it receives dappled shade for part of the day.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in sharply drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade; 'Wood's Compact' forms a tighter, lower mat than the species and is often recommended where a neater groundcover edge is wanted.

directions: Plant rooted container stock in spring in sharply drained, acidic, infertile sandy soil, spacing closer together than standard bearberry since this selection stays denser and shorter. 'Wood's Compact' is valued by home gardeners and extension programs for a tidier, slower-creeping habit that still forms a continuous evergreen carpet within a couple of seasons. Small pink-tinged spring flowers give way to bright red berries held through winter, important for grouse, foxes, and other wildlife, and edible but dry and bland for fresh eating. Avoid fertilizer, irrigation, or rich mulches, all of which encourage root rot in this drought- and poverty-soil-adapted selection.
